sources.citation: Carter, Jed, Beautlyn Eliab, Karl Kama, Roger Maikei, Devin O'Bannon & Napa Yanderave. 2023. Survey Report for Uma (Ronji) [roe], Tandɨ (Yagomi) [ygm], Muratayak [asx], Degenang (Degenan) [dge], and Forak [frq] Languages. Journal of Language Survey Reports 2023-003. Dallas: SIL International. 71 pp.
sources.note: Nothing: the words stress/accent/tone/syllable do not occur; 0 IPA stress marks in the text, confirmed visually on p. 62 (printed p. 56). Sec. 1.1.4 (Degenang in Seure and Sel; varieties Degenang and Sidbi/Andik), sec. 1.2.3 (prior research = Claassen 1968/1969a wordlists only), sec. 2.1.4 (120-item SIL-PNG list 'transcribed using the IPA and digitally recorded'); App. D Table 37 (printed pp. 55-64) Degenang (Sel) and Sidbi/Andik (Seure) columns in IPA with vowel length but no stress marks (tɘnam 'his head', namet 'ear', meleŋ 'tongue', menɘp 'tooth', dorɘk 'blood', umalep 'man', mɘnam 'bird'…

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2018. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics 4), 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: For Degenan only the documentation status ('wordlist: Carter et al. 2012'). The chapter's prosody section (after Donohue 1997, Ross 2005) has one family-level sentence: 'In languages of the Madang and Finisterre-Huon groups and of South-east Papua generally, tone and pitch accent are largely absent.' - a secondhand areal generalization, not a statement about Degenan, and it says nothing about stress placement.

sources.citation: Carter, John, Katie Carter, John Grummitt, Bonnie MacKenzie & Janell Masters. 2012. A sociolinguistic survey of the Mur village vernaculars. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2012-043. Dallas: SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing for Degenan. Degenan appears as Mur's neighbour (Sel 5 km SE) and as a 40-item ASJP comparison column (App., printed pp. 49-50: village Sel, elicitor O. Claassen, subject Siga 26-M, 16-Dec-68, reliability fair-good; mənʌm 'bird', dor̃uk 'blood', mumʌŋ 'breast' -- no stress marks); Molet-Degenan lexicostat 21-23%. App. B phonological notes cover Mur Pano and Mur Molet only.

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald. 2012. Pronouns and the (preliminary) classification of Papuan languages. In Harald Hammarström & Wilco van den Heuvel (eds.), History, contact and classification of Papuan languages (Language & Linguistics in Melanesia Special Issue 2012, Part II), 428-539. Port Moresby: Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing. Degenan occurs exactly once in the 113-page article, in the Appendix classification of Papuan languages (printed p. 503) as a bare entry 'Degenan [dge]' in the Warup group; unlike its neighbours (e.g. 'Wantoat-Awara Hooley and McElhanon (1970:1074)', 'Ma [mjn] Z'graggen (1975:9)') it carries no pronoun-source citation, i.e. no Degenan pronoun forms entered the study. The body is a statistical argument about chance resemblances among pronoun forms (contra Ross 1995, 2001, 2005); it contains no phonological description of any Finisterre language, and the strings stress/accent/tone/pros…

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew. 2001. The Proto Trans New Guinea obstruents: arguments from top-down reconstruction. In Andrew Pawley, Malcolm Ross & Darrell Tryon (eds.), The boy from Bundaberg: Studies in Melanesian linguistics in honour of Tom Dutton, 261-300. Pacific Linguistics 514. Canberra: Australian National University. (ANU Open Research hdl 1885/254062, doi 10.15144/PL-514.261, CC BY-SA)
sources.note: No Degenan phonology: Degenan occurs only twice, as the Warup witness in cognate set 5 *mbutu 'wing' ('F-H War Degenan pur', printed p. 276) and set 17 *kambu(s,t)(a,u) 'smoke' ('F-H War Degenan gdbi' in the text, vowel symbol garbled, p. 278). The paper treats segmental correspondences only; its single prosodic remark is family-wide: 'A number of TNG languages are tonal, with considerable typological variety in the systems (Donohue 1997), but only segmental phonemes will be considered here' (p. 271). Nothing on Degenan stress, accent or tone; no stress marks on the two cited forms.

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90. Canberra: Australian National University. xiii+476 pp.
sources.note: Bibliographic pointer only: works indexed for Degenan up to 1995 are Claassen & McElhanon 1970, W&H 1981 (Wurm & Hattori atlas) and Z'graggen 1975; the author entry 'CLAASSEN, Oren R. n.d. Field notes, Gusap-Mot and Warup families' records the unpublished SIL field notes (Ukarumpa) already on our list of works to obtain. Confirms that no grammar, phonology or sketch of Degenan existed by 1996.

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1975. North-eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In Wurm (ed.), PL C-38, 527-567.
sources.note: Checklist only: '2.8.1.3.7.6. Degenan (WR-52), pop. 500. Warup Census Division: Mur, Sel, and Seure.' Nothing on phonology.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, John A. 1975. The languages of the Madang District, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-41. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology content for Degenan: village census and classification only ('A10 Degenan 358: Sel (250) 210, Seure 148'; Sel also has Arop [Austronesian] speakers; Mamgak = A9 Forak). The volume has no phonological notes for the Finisterre (non-Madang-Adelbert) languages.

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1973. Towards a typology of the Finisterre-Huon languages, New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-22. Canberra: ANU.
sources.harvard_location: Divinity School Library (offsite storage), call number - Ask at Circulation (Pamph. folio) BS 354 .Z91
sources.note: Degenan only in the language list (Warup Family a.); ch. 1 phonology compares ten representative languages (none Warup) and contains no stress/accent statement at all.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range - New Guinea. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11, 45-78. Pacific Linguistics A-23. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 (p. 53) locates Degenan (~300 speakers, Sel/Seure; Mamgak possibly a divergent dialect). Sec. 6.1 Phonology (pp. 63-66) treats one representative language per family and includes NO Warup-family language; its only stress remarks (p. 66) concern Rawa ('phonemic'), Yupna and Wantoat ('probably sub-phonemic') and Suroi. Silent on Degenan stress.

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. & C. L. Voorhoeve. 1970. The Trans-New Guinea Phylum: explorations in deep-level genetic relationships. Pacific Linguistics B-16. Canberra: Australian National University. 112 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 1.6: 'Most of the data used in this study has not yet been phonemicized; the spelling is therefore phonetic and for practical reasons follows Pike 1947' (the phonemicized exceptions are Ok, Asmat, Gogodala, Suki, Sentani - not Finisterre-Huon). Degenan forms appear only as 'WAR a' items inside the cognate sets (e.g. kara 'arm', doruk 'blood', tAnam 'head', got 'hair', dabal 'eye', ogutur 'fingernail', imdam 'knee', mor 'mouth', merr- 'skin'), typed without any stress or pitch marks; no remark on stress, accent or tone for any Finisterre-Huon language. Wordlist-level data only, no stateme…

sources.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. 1970. The Selepet language within the Finisterre-Huon phylum (New Guinea). PhD thesis, Australian National University. xii+487 pp. (ANU Open Research, hdl 1885/109875)
sources.note: lexicostatistical percentages only; all stress statements in the thesis (predictable primary stress on the initial syllable of the stress group, 'Since stress is predictable it is left unmarked') concern Selepet alone
